name: Shibuya
summary: The pulsing heart of young Tokyo — Scramble Crossing, Shibuya Sky, department stores, and hundreds of bars and clubs packed into walkable streets.
description: Start at Hachikō statue, sweep across the crossing, and fan out into Center Gai for vintage, Dogenzaka for clubs, or Cat Street for quieter shops toward Harajuku. Shibuya Sky (free-standing open-air observation deck) is the best sunset spot in the city.
transit_hubs: Shibuya Station (JR Yamanote, Ginza / Hanzomon / Fukutoshin lines)

name: Shinjuku
summary: Home to the world's busiest station and everything from skyline bars to Golden Gai's 200 shoebox-sized pubs. Kabukichō is the red-light fringe — lively but watch for touts.
description: East side is neon, food, and nightlife (Golden Gai, Omoide Yokocho). West side is skyscrapers with free observation decks at the Metropolitan Government Building. South side has Shinjuku Gyoen for decompressing. Ni-chōme just past Kabukichō is Asia's densest LGBTQ nightlife strip.

name: Ginza
summary: Tokyo's luxury boulevard — flagship fashion houses, Michelin sushi counters, and Kabukiza theatre, all with a calmer pace than the youthful hubs.
description: Chūō-dōri, the main street, is pedestrianised on weekends (hokōsha tengoku). Stop at Itoya for stationery nerdery, Ginza Six for luxury + a top-floor rooftop garden, and Ginza Kyubey or Sukiyabashi Jiro Roppongi branch for the big sushi experience. Kabukiza theatre offers single-act tickets (¥1,500-¥2,500).

name: Asakusa
summary: Old Tokyo vibes anchored by Sensō-ji temple. Best visited at dawn or after 18:00 when the Nakamise-dōri shopping street thins.
description: Beyond Sensō-ji, walk the covered arcades for senbei (rice crackers) and tenugui (hand towels). Cross the river to Tokyo Skytree. Hop on a Sumida River cruise to Hamarikyū or Odaiba. Kappabashi's kitchenware street is nearby.
transit_hubs: Asakusa Station (Ginza, Asakusa, Tobu Skytree lines)

name: Harajuku
summary: Youth fashion, crêperies, and the ceremonial entrance to Meiji Jingū — Harajuku runs from sacred to sugar-rush in the span of 500 metres.
description: Takeshita-dōri is the rainbow-cotton-candy tourist lane; Ura-Harajuku is the indie side street grid with quieter coffee and vintage. Omotesandō continues south as Tokyo's 'Champs-Élysées' — Prada Aoyama, Dior, Louis Vuitton flagships. Meiji Jingū's forest sits right next door.

name: Akihabara
summary: Neon-lit Electric Town with Super Potato (retro games), Mandarake (vintage manga and figures), and Yodobashi-Akiba's mega electronics floors.
description: Chūō-dōri is pedestrian on Sundays. Stick to reputable shops and skip the 'free drink' invitations from street promoters — the reputable maid cafés like @home put their prices plainly outside. Try 2K540 near Okachimachi for craft workshops.
transit_hubs: Akihabara Station (JR Yamanote, Hibiya, Tsukuba Express)

name: Roppongi
summary: Where Tokyo's international scene lives and plays. Three world-class museums form the 'Art Triangle', while the streets below keep going past 03:00.
description: Mori Art Museum on the 53rd floor of Roppongi Hills is the Tokyo skyline plus contemporary art in one ticket. The National Art Center has no permanent collection but hosts the city's biggest touring shows. Avoid club touts — if you're nudged in, you'll likely be overcharged.

name: Daikanyama & Nakameguro
summary: Low-rise, tree-lined, and independent. Tsutaya's flagship bookstore complex, hidden menswear boutiques, and the Meguro River — Tokyo's most photographed cherry-blossom canal.
description: Daikanyama T-Site (Tsutaya) is worth 90 minutes for magazines, stationery, and a great café. Walk 12 minutes down to Nakameguro for riverside cafés and shops. In late March / early April the river glows with pink illuminations at night.

name: Shimokitazawa
summary: Tokyo's Brooklyn, 10 minutes from Shinjuku — narrow alleys packed with vintage stores, tiny live-house venues, and third-wave coffee.
description: Spend an afternoon thrifting at Flamingo, Chicago, and Stick-Out; dinner at Shirube for creative izakaya; late set at Club Que or Basement Bar. The new Reload complex brings designer shops to the formerly scruffy north side.

name: Yanaka
summary: One of the few districts to survive World War II bombing — low wooden houses, small temples, and a stray-cat population that inspired a resident cat guidebook.
description: Yanaka Ginza shopping street is best at 17:00 as croquette and skewer shops ramp up. Wander the cemetery (peaceful, with cherry trees). Take an old-fashioned public bath at Daikoku-yu. Walk to Nezu Shrine's orange torii tunnel for the underrated alternative to Kyoto's Fushimi Inari.

name: Tsukiji & Toyosu
summary: The Outer Market in Tsukiji is the retail food-tour heart; the wholesale action moved east to Toyosu in 2018, now open to visitors via a viewing gallery.
description: Tsukiji Outer Market is best 07:00-10:00 — grilled scallops, tamagoyaki skewers, knife shops, Sushi Dai. Toyosu Market (a 15-minute Yurikamome ride) has tuna-auction viewing decks; Senkyaku Banrai rooftop onsen opened in 2024 above the market.

name: Odaiba
summary: Man-made island in Tokyo Bay with beaches, Rainbow Bridge views, shopping malls, and the life-sized Unicorn Gundam statue that moves on the hour.
description: Take the driverless Yurikamome train from Shimbashi for the ride itself. DiverCity Tokyo Plaza has the Gundam and a large mall; Aqua City is the mall with the best Rainbow Bridge view. teamLab Planets is a short walk from the Odaiba peninsula at Toyosu.
